transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hey Dr. Smith. Yeah, thanks for seeing me. I mean, it was a whole thing just getting my schedule cleared to get here today, but I knew I had to come in because things are just getting out of hand at work. I'm an electrician, mostly residential with some light commercial, and usually I'm pretty dialed in. I have to be, you know? You mess up a wire, you fail an inspection, or worse. 

But lately, what finally got me to actually make this appointment is that I just can’t keep my focus on one estimate or code form anymore. It's driving me crazy. I'll sit down at my desk to write up a quote—which is tedious anyway, but I used to just bang them out in twenty minutes—and I just can't stay on it. If I hear a tool noise from the guys out in the bay, like a drill or a saw, I'm completely derailed. Or my phone will buzz with a text, and I'll look at it, and suddenly that triggers some entirely new idea about how we need to reorganize the workshop or build a new shelving unit for the conduit. So I'll get up and start sketching that out on a piece of scrap drywall, completely forgetting the paperwork. 

And because I keep getting pulled off track by every little sound or thought, jobs are starting to get mixed up. I'll put the specs for one house onto the invoice for another, or forget which client wanted the upgraded panel. It's getting really messy, and I can't afford to be making those kinds of rookie mistakes just because my brain is bouncing off every little thing happening in the room.
Has this kind of distractibility and trouble focusing been something you've dealt with since childhood or your teenage years, or is this a new change from how you normally are?

No, no, see, that's the crazy part about all this. It's completely new. I mean... if you look back at when I was a kid, or even a teenager in high school, I wasn't exactly some straight-A student who loved sitting at a desk all day. That's actually why I only did a little bit of college before I realized I really just needed to be working with my hands. But I never, ever had trouble actually focusing when I needed to get something done. 

Like, when I was going through my apprenticeship? You have to learn the National Electrical Code inside and out. It's this massive, incredibly dry book—just hundreds of pages of pure technical jargon, wire gauges, conduit fill capacities, grounding requirements, all that stuff. And I could sit at my kitchen table for three, four hours straight with a yellow highlighter and just drill it into my brain. I'd be totally locked in. My old boss used to joke that I had tunnel vision when I was working on a tricky circuit. If I was tracing a fault in a wall, you could literally drop a hammer right next to me on the floor and I wouldn't even flinch. I was just... you know, dialed in. 

So to go from being that kind of guy—the guy who can tune out an entire noisy construction site just to figure out a wiring issue—to whatever is happening to me right now? It's like night and day. Now, I swear, a fly buzzes past my head and I'm suddenly wondering if the shop window screens need replacing, and then I'm looking up aluminum mesh materials on my phone, and twenty minutes later I haven't even looked at the quote I was supposed to be writing. So yeah, it's definitely a massive change. I've never been like this before in my life, not even close.

Along with this distractibility, have you noticed any changes in your mood or energy—like feeling unusually elated, irritable, or like you have way more energy than usual, or needing much less sleep than you normally would?

Yeah, actually, that's... that's a big part of it, too. The energy thing. It's like I'm running on a 220 line when everyone else is on 110, you know? I'll wake up and I just feel... I don't know, huge. Like I'm completely pumped up, just buzzing with all these ideas. I'll get to the shop and I'll start telling the guys, like, "Listen, we're not just doing panel upgrades anymore. We need to pivot. We're going to corner the market on residential solar installs in this whole tri-county area." And I'll have this whole grand vision mapped out in my head about how we're going to expand the fleet, re-wrap the vans, hire three new crews, and I'm just talking and talking because it feels so clear to me. It feels amazing, honestly. Like I'm finally seeing the big picture and we're about to strike gold.

But... the problem is, if anyone pushes back even a little bit, it just sets me off. Like, my wife came by the shop the other day to drop off lunch, and I was in the middle of explaining this massive solar expansion to her, and she just asked a simple question. Something like, "Well, do the guys even have the certifications for that yet?" And man, I just... I snapped. I flipped a switch. I got so incredibly sharp with her, just laying into her about how she wasn't seeing the vision, how she was dragging me down with small-minded details. And it's not just her. If one of the apprentices hesitates when I tell him to go pull all the inventory for this big imaginary project, I'll just lose it on him. I'll get so irritable over absolutely nothing, just because they aren't keeping up with my pace. It's like I'm on top of the world one second, and the next second I'm biting someone's head off because they asked a totally reasonable question.

Before this recent change, have you ever had a period—lasting a week or more—where you felt unusually low, depressed, or lost interest in things, or another time where you felt this same kind of high energy and grand thinking?

No, honestly, I don't think so. I mean, I'm trying to think back over the last few years, or even back to my early twenties when I first started working in the trade, and I really can't remember anything like this happening before. I've definitely never had this kind of crazy energy where I'm ready to take over the world and buy out all my competitors. This whole solar empire idea, the re-wrapping the vans, the snapping at my wife—that is all 100% brand new. It's like I just woke up a couple of weeks ago and someone had flipped a breaker in my brain that I didn't even know was there. 

And as for feeling low or depressed... I mean, look, construction has its ups and downs, right? You have slow seasons, especially in the winter, and sometimes you get a little stressed about money or keeping the guys busy. There was that one time a few years ago when supply chain issues were holding up all our copper wire and I was pretty stressed out for a couple of weeks, maybe a little bummed out that jobs were stalling. But it wasn't like what you see on those commercials where you can't get out of bed or you hate your life. I still got up every day, I still went to the shop, I still liked having a beer with my buddies on the weekend. I never had a whole week where I just felt completely empty or stopped caring about my job. I've always been pretty steady. Just a normal guy, working hard, paying the bills. So yeah, this whole extreme high thing, and the distractibility... it's completely out of left field for me. I've never had a high like this, and I've never really had a real low either.

Have you experienced anything like hearing voices or sounds that others don't seem to hear, or holding beliefs—like being destined for extraordinary success or having special abilities—that others have told you seem unrealistic or out of touch with reality?

Voices? No, no, definitely not hearing things. I mean, my ears ring sometimes from years of running impact drivers and hammer drills without earplugs, but no, no voices or anything like that. 

But as for the... the beliefs, or thinking I'm meant for something bigger? Yeah. Yeah, that's exactly what I've been trying to explain with the whole solar empire thing, but honestly, it goes even further than that. 

See, lately, I just have this absolute certainty—like, this rock-solid feeling in my chest—that I can take on these massive commercial jobs. And I'm not talking about wiring up a little strip mall bakery or something. I'm talking about the big industrial stuff, the massive high-rises they're putting up downtown. I'll drive past those sites and I just think, "I should be running that site." I feel like I could walk in there right now, today, take over the blueprints, and train a whole crew of twenty guys to do it perfectly. I'll start telling the guys at the shop about it, just pacing around the supply room going, "We're going commercial, boys, we're going to bid on that new hospital wing." 

And they just look at me like I've completely lost my mind. Because, you know, if I'm being completely honest with myself... well, part of me knows that my licensing and my actual experience aren't quite where they need to be for all that. You need different insurance, different bonding, and I've only ever really managed maybe two or three apprentices at a time, mostly doing residential panel swaps and pulling Romex through attics. Commercial is a whole different beast, right? It's three-phase power, heavy-duty switchgear, bending rigid metal conduit all day long. 

But when I get in these moods, when my brain is just firing on all cylinders like it has been, none of that matters to me. The lack of experience, the licensing red tape—it just feels like minor details, just little speed bumps I can easily swat out of the way. I just feel so incredibly capable, like I'm the only guy in the state who really understands how to put a massive grid together, even though my logical brain is sitting in the backseat going, "Hey man, you've never even wired a commercial elevator shaft before." It doesn't matter. I just can't shake the feeling that I'm completely unstoppable right now, and anyone who tells me it's unrealistic just isn't thinking big enough.

Have you actually gone ahead and taken concrete steps—like submitting a bid, signing a contract, or spending money—on one of these big commercial projects, even though part of you knew you didn't have the license or experience for it?

Well, see, the thing about the commercial contracts is... I haven't actually put ink to paper on a high-rise downtown yet, no. I haven't spent the money on the commercial bonding just yet. But as far as taking steps? Man, I am doing bids. I'm doing so many bids, just maybe not the hospital wing today. 

It's just... I've been going absolutely nonstop, honestly. From the second I wake up, I'm just blasting from residential job sites to hammering out bids on my tablet in the truck, and then back to the shop. And when I get to the shop, even after the apprentices pack up and go home for the day, I can't just clock out. I can't do it. Sitting still right now... it literally feels like I'm wasting time. Like I'm just throwing my life away if I'm not producing something or building this empire. 

So I'll be alone in the workshop for hours, and I'm just rewiring these complex test panels, trying to prep for when we *do* get those bigger jobs. Just stripping wire, bending conduit, testing loads. And then, right in the middle of that, I'll get this brilliant idea for, like, a custom home-automation setup. I'll start mapping out how to integrate a client's lighting with their HVAC on a single smart relay system, pulling all the components off the shelves, getting everything laid out... but before that one is even halfway done, my brain is already onto the next thing, and I'm starting on a totally new home-automation idea for, I don't know, remote solar-powered security gates. 

My workbench is just an absolute disaster zone right now. It's covered in half-finished projects, wire clippings everywhere, relays stacked up, because I just keep moving, moving, moving. Job sites to bids to rewiring test panels to starting new automation ideas before the last one is even screwed into the wall... it's just a constant, endless stream of action. I just have to be doing something, you know? If I stop, I feel like I'm going to explode. So yeah, I'm definitely taking steps, I'm doing a million things at once right now.

doctor.question: Have you experienced anything like hearing voices or sounds that others don't seem to hear, or holding beliefs—like being destined for extraordinary success or having special abilities—that others have told you seem unrealistic or out of touch with reality?

target_item.name: Inflated_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: I keep feeling like I can take on commercial jobs and train a whole crew right now, even though part of me knows my licensing and experience aren’t quite where they need to be for all that.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about grandiose beliefs or delusions, which directly corresponds to the symptom of inflated self-esteem or grandiosity.

patient.answer:
Voices? No, no, definitely not hearing things. I mean, my ears ring sometimes from years of running impact drivers and hammer drills without earplugs, but no, no voices or anything like that. 

But as for the... the beliefs, or thinking I'm meant for something bigger? Yeah. Yeah, that's exactly what I've been trying to explain with the whole solar empire thing, but honestly, it goes even further than that. 

See, lately, I just have this absolute certainty—like, this rock-solid feeling in my chest—that I can take on these massive commercial jobs. And I'm not talking about wiring up a little strip mall bakery or something. I'm talking about the big industrial stuff, the massive high-rises they're putting up downtown. I'll drive past those sites and I just think, "I should be running that site." I feel like I could walk in there right now, today, take over the blueprints, and train a whole crew of twenty guys to do it perfectly. I'll start telling the guys at the shop about it, just pacing around the supply room going, "We're going commercial, boys, we're going to bid on that new hospital wing." 

And they just look at me like I've completely lost my mind. Because, you know, if I'm being completely honest with myself... well, part of me knows that my licensing and my actual experience aren't quite where they need to be for all that. You need different insurance, different bonding, and I've only ever really managed maybe two or three apprentices at a time, mostly doing residential panel swaps and pulling Romex through attics. Commercial is a whole different beast, right? It's three-phase power, heavy-duty switchgear, bending rigid metal conduit all day long. 

But when I get in these moods, when my brain is just firing on all cylinders like it has been, none of that matters to me. The lack of experience, the licensing red tape—it just feels like minor details, just little speed bumps I can easily swat out of the way. I just feel so incredibly capable, like I'm the only guy in the state who really understands how to put a massive grid together, even though my logical brain is sitting in the backseat going, "Hey man, you've never even wired a commercial elevator shaft before." It doesn't matter. I just can't shake the feeling that I'm completely unstoppable right now, and anyone who tells me it's unrealistic just isn't thinking big enough.

inference.note: Grandiose beliefs (running commercial high-rises, being 'unstoppable') are more extreme than simple overconfidence, raising suspicion for mood-congruent grandiose delusions, though patient still shows partial insight ('logical brain in the backseat'). This keeps both non-psychotic and psychotic manic episode codes in play; no hallucinations reported, and no prior mood episodes support ruling out bipolar disorder codes.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the grandiose beliefs are fixed and acted upon despite full awareness of contrary reality (suggesting psychotic-level conviction) versus remaining a grandiose but reality-testable idea, which helps distinguish mania with psychotic features (F30.2) from hypomania/mania without psychotic features (F30.1)
doctor.question: Have you actually gone ahead and taken concrete steps—like submitting a bid, signing a contract, or spending money—on one of these big commercial projects, even though part of you knew you didn't have the license or experience for it?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been going nonstop from job sites to bids to rewiring test panels in the workshop, starting new home-automation ideas before the last one is done because sitting still feels like wasting time.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about concrete steps and actions taken towards these grand ideas (submitting bids, signing contracts), which corresponds to the increased goal-directed activity and energy described in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, see, the thing about the commercial contracts is... I haven't actually put ink to paper on a high-rise downtown yet, no. I haven't spent the money on the commercial bonding just yet. But as far as taking steps? Man, I am doing bids. I'm doing so many bids, just maybe not the hospital wing today. 

It's just... I've been going absolutely nonstop, honestly. From the second I wake up, I'm just blasting from residential job sites to hammering out bids on my tablet in the truck, and then back to the shop. And when I get to the shop, even after the apprentices pack up and go home for the day, I can't just clock out. I can't do it. Sitting still right now... it literally feels like I'm wasting time. Like I'm just throwing my life away if I'm not producing something or building this empire. 

So I'll be alone in the workshop for hours, and I'm just rewiring these complex test panels, trying to prep for when we *do* get those bigger jobs. Just stripping wire, bending conduit, testing loads. And then, right in the middle of that, I'll get this brilliant idea for, like, a custom home-automation setup. I'll start mapping out how to integrate a client's lighting with their HVAC on a single smart relay system, pulling all the components off the shelves, getting everything laid out... but before that one is even halfway done, my brain is already onto the next thing, and I'm starting on a totally new home-automation idea for, I don't know, remote solar-powered security gates. 

My workbench is just an absolute disaster zone right now. It's covered in half-finished projects, wire clippings everywhere, relays stacked up, because I just keep moving, moving, moving. Job sites to bids to rewiring test panels to starting new automation ideas before the last one is even screwed into the wall... it's just a constant, endless stream of action. I just have to be doing something, you know? If I stop, I feel like I'm going to explode. So yeah, I'm definitely taking steps, I'm doing a million things at once right now.

inference.note: Patient retains partial insight into unrealistic nature of grandiose beliefs ('my logical brain is sitting in the backseat') and has not acted on delusional-level certainty, indicating grandiosity without frank psychotic delusions. This rules out F30.2 (severe manic episode with psychotic features), leaving F30.1 (severe manic episode without psychotic features) as the best fit given marked impairment, irritability, decreased need for rest, and excessive goal-directed activity.
